summary.title: Three-dimensional topological valley photonics
summary.authors: Wenhao Li, Qiaolu Chen, Ning Han, Xinrui Li, Fujia Chen, Junyao Wu, Yuang Pan, Yudong Ren, Hongsheng Chen, Haoran Xue, Yihao Yang
summary.executive_summary: Topological valley photonics exploits the valley degree of freedom to control electromagnetic waves, but prior work has been confined to two dimensions, where photonic confinement along the third dimension is usually achieved in a non-topological way such as total internal reflection. Such 2D systems support single-polarization valley states, suffer from out-of-plane losses, and can only manipulate light flow in planar geometries. Full confinement and full control of light flow require a complete photonic bandgap, in which light of any polarization is forbidden to propagate in any direction in three dimensions, and this remains a significant challenge. This paper introduces a theoretical and experimental framework of three-dimensional (3D) topological valley photonics with a complete photonic bandgap and vectorial valley-contrasting physics. The 3D valley systems exhibit triple pairs of valleys characterized by valley Chern vectors, enabling vectorial bulk valley vortices and canalized chiral valley surface states. The valley Chern vectors and the circulating propagation direction of the valley surface states are intrinsically governed by the right-hand-thumb rule. The authors use a 3D photonic crystal with lattice constant a = 20 mm, built from perfect electric conductor spheres and rods, and break inversion symmetry by setting D1 = 6.4 mm and D2 = 3.6 mm to open a complete bandgap. They verify vectorial valley-contrasting Berry curvature using a vectorial chiral source array and pump-probe measurements, and demonstrate robust canalized valley surface states on all surfaces of a shaped sample. The measured outcoupling directions at 13.8 GHz are −32.9°, 0°, and +32.9°, corresponding to Wy−, X, and Wy+. The surface states propagate diffractionlessly along +y corresponding to the Wx− valley, and the right-hand-thumb rule is confirmed across (001) and (010) surfaces. The findings highlight applications in 3D waveguiding, directional radiation, and imaging, and suggest extension to terahertz and optical ranges.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
Topological valley photonics exploits the valley degree of freedom to control electromagnetic waves, but prior work has been confined to two dimensions, where photonic confinement along the third dimension is usually achieved in a non-topological way such as total internal reflection. Such 2D systems support single-polarization valley states, suffer from out-of-plane losses, and can only manipulate light flow in planar geometries. Full confinement and full control of light flow require a complete photonic bandgap, in which light of any polarization is forbidden to propagate in any direction in three dimensions, and this remains a significant challenge. This paper introduces a theoretical and experimental framework of three-dimensional (3D) topological valley photonics with a complete photonic bandgap and vectorial valley-contrasting physics. The 3D valley systems exhibit triple pairs of valleys characterized by valley Chern vectors, enabling vectorial bulk valley vortices and canalized chiral valley surface states. The valley Chern vectors and the circulating propagation direction of the valley surface states are intrinsically governed by the right-hand-thumb rule. The authors use a 3D photonic crystal with lattice constant a = 20 mm, built from perfect electric conductor spheres and rods, and break inversion symmetry by setting D1 = 6.4 mm and D2 = 3.6 mm to open a complete bandgap. They verify vectorial valley-contrasting Berry curvature using a vectorial chiral source array and pump-probe measurements, and demonstrate robust canalized valley surface states on all surfaces of a shaped sample. The measured outcoupling directions at 13.8 GHz are −32.9°, 0°, and +32.9°, corresponding to Wy−, X, and Wy+. The surface states propagate diffractionlessly along +y corresponding to the Wx− valley, and the right-hand-thumb rule is confirmed across (001) and (010) surfaces. The findings highlight applications in 3D waveguiding, directional radiation, and imaging, and suggest extension to terahertz and optical ranges.

Research Context
Valley photonics supplements conventional degrees of freedom to control light. 2D valley photonic crystals host a single pair of valleys with scalar invariants. Valley-contrasting physics underlies vortex states and edge states. VPCs are experimentally feasible without breaking time-reversal symmetry. Prior valley photonics is limited to two dimensions. 2D systems suffer from out-of-plane losses and planar confinement. Full confinement requires a complete photonic bandgap. A complete bandgap remains a significant challenge.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can 3D topological valley photonics be realized with a complete bandgap? Do 3D valley systems exhibit triple pairs of valleys with vectorial invariants? Are valley Chern vectors the governing vectorial invariant? Do vectorial bulk valley vortices and canalized chiral surface states arise? Is the propagation governed by the right-hand-thumb rule? Can valley surface states be canalized on all sample surfaces? Can valley states be selectively excited by chirality-matched sources?

Methodological Details
The study is both theoretical and experimental. The 3D photonic crystal has lattice constant a = 20 mm. Lattice vectors are a1 = (a/2, a/2, 0), a2 = (0, a/2, a/2), a3 = (a/2, 0, a/2). The crystal is a photonic diamond with PEC spheres and rods. Each fcc cell contains two spheres with diameters D1 and D2. Nearest spheres are connected by PEC rods with diameter B1 = 2.4 mm. Next-nearest spheres are connected by PEC rods with diameter B2 = 1.2 mm. B2 rods suppress high-order modes for a clean bandstructure. Inversion symmetry is preserved when D1 = D2 = 5 mm. Inversion symmetry is broken when D1 = 6.4 mm and D2 = 3.6 mm. The broken symmetry gaps out nodal lines to form a complete bandgap. The six valleys are located at Wx±, Wy±, and Wz±.

Procedures And Architectures
The band structure is computed and shown in Fig. 1(b). Nodal chains form along Wα±-X when ∆D = 0. The valley momenta are (±π/a, 2π/a, 0), (0, ±π/a, 2π/a), and (2π/a, 0, ±π/a). The effective Hamiltonian is derived by the k · p method. The mass term is m = (ω1 − ω2)/2 from broken inversion symmetry. The vectorial chiral source array uses four sources. Source positions are (0, 0, 0), (−a/2, −a/2, 0), (−a/2, 0, −a/2), and (0, −a/2, −a/2). Phase delays are (0, π/2, π, 3π/2) for Wy− and (0, −π/2, −π, −3π/2) for Wy+. The valley Chern vector is integrated over a planar region around each valley. The VCVs are (±1/2, 0, 0), (0, ±1/2, 0), and (0, 0, ±1/2). The boundary condition uses τz = σy sin θV + σz cos θV. The surface is covered by a metallic plate with perforations of interval a/2.

Key Results
The Berry curvature has nonzero component only in the kx-ky plane. The measured outcoupling directions at 13.8 GHz are −32.9°, 0°, and +32.9°. The clockwise and counterclockwise windings correspond to −32.9° and +32.9°. The no-winding case corresponds to 0° at X. The radiated beams are single-directional in 3D space. The VCVs are (±1/2, 0, 0), (0, ±1/2, 0), and (0, 0, ±1/2). The surface states traverse the bandgap with linear dispersion. The surface transmission stays high within the complete bandgap. The surface states propagate canalization along +y for the Wx− valley. The isofrequency contours are flat, confirmed experimentally and numerically. The surface states exist on all (100), (010), and (001) surfaces. The propagation direction is locked to each valley without intervalley scattering.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The vectorial nature of 3D valley states is revealed. The valley Chern vectors and propagation direction obey the right-hand-thumb rule. The rule is an intrinsic relation determined by the bulk Hamiltonian. The canalization is an intrinsic property of the surface states. The surface states offer opportunities for imaging and lensing. The orbital moments provide a means to control the angular momentum of light. The directional outcoupling can create narrow-beam antennae. The concept can be extended to terahertz and optical ranges.

Contradictions And Limitations
The demonstration is at lower frequencies. The concept can be extended to higher frequencies. The exact operating frequency is not uniformly stated across figures. The sample shape is required for surface states on all surfaces. The boundary condition relies on tuning D3 and h. The random seed and train/test split are not applicable to this physics study.

Claims
3D topological valley photonics with a complete photonic bandgap and vectorial valley-contrasting physics is realized. The framework is both theoretical and experimental. The complete bandgap forbids propagation of any polarization in 3D. The 3D systems exhibit triple pairs of valleys. The Berry curvature has nonzero component only in the kx-ky plane. Prior valley photonics is limited to 2D systems. 2D systems suffer from out-of-plane losses. The concept can be extended to terahertz and optical ranges. The framework enables 3D waveguiding, directional radiation, and imaging.
Vectorial valley-contrasting Berry curvature enables selective excitation of chiral valley states. The vectorial chiral source array uses four sources. The measured outcoupling directions are −32.9°, 0°, and +32.9°. The radiated beams are single-directional in 3D space. The 2D radiation pattern diverges in the vertical direction. The directional outcoupling can serve as a mechanism for narrow-beam antennae.
Robust canalized chiral valley surface states exist on all sample surfaces. The surface states exist on all (100), (010), and (001) surfaces. The surface states propagate canalization along +y for the Wx− valley. The isofrequency contours are flat, confirmed experimentally and numerically. Existing 3D topological photonic insulators support surface states on certain surfaces only. The canalization offers opportunities for imaging and lensing.
The right-hand-thumb rule relates valley Chern vectors to the circulating direction of valley surface states. The rule is confirmed across (001) and (010) surfaces. The rule is an intrinsic relation determined by the bulk Hamiltonian. The propagation direction is locked to each valley without intervalley scattering. The exact operating frequency is not uniformly stated across figures. The rule enables valley conservation through sharp corners.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The B2 rods suppress high-order modes for a clean bandstructure. The boundary condition is satisfied when h = 6.25 mm and D3 = 4 mm. The canalization is confirmed both experimentally and numerically. The valley-locking property is revealed experimentally.

Key Figures Tables
Fig. 1 shows the 3D VPC, band structure, valleys, and Berry curvature. Fig. 2 shows selective excitation of vectorial valley states. Fig. 3 shows canalized chiral valley surface states. Fig. 4 shows the right-hand-thumb rule relating VCVs and surface states.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a 3D topological valley photonics framework with a complete bandgap and vectorial valley-contrasting physics. 2. The strongest evidence is the canalized chiral valley surface states on all surfaces obeying the right-hand-thumb rule. 3. The future path is extending the concept to terahertz and optical ranges with all-dielectric crystals.
